title: IIT Bombay-Incubated InspeCity Raises Rs 100 Crore to Build Satellite Service Stations in Space
excerpt: The spacetech startup plans four in-orbit missions over the next 18 months to prove its autonomous satellite-servicing technology, with backing from Speciale Invest and investor Ashish Kacholia.
body:
• IIT Bombay-incubated InspeCity has raised Rs 100 crore ($10.5 million) in a pre-Series A round led by Speciale Invest and investor Ashish Kacholia.
  • The startup builds autonomous systems to inspect, refuel, repair and deorbit satellites already in space — essentially roadside assistance for spacecraft.
  • InspeCity plans to execute four in-orbit missions over the next 12 to 18 months to validate its integrated technology stack.
  • The raise comes as Indian spacetech attracts record capital, with Skyroot Aerospace becoming the country's first spacetech unicorn earlier this year.

InspeCity, a spacetech startup incubated at IIT Bombay, has raised Rs 100 crore (approximately $10.5 million) in a pre-Series A funding round as it prepares to send its satellite-servicing technology into orbit. The round was co-led by Speciale Invest and investor Ashish Kacholia, with participation from Antler Elevate, Antler India, Manish Gandhi and Shastra VC.

The raise more than doubles the company's total funding. InspeCity picked up $5.6 million in seed funding in May 2025, also led by Kacholia, and $1.5 million in a pre-seed round before that.

What InspeCity Actually Does

Unlike most Indian space startups that build rockets or satellites, InspeCity focuses on what happens after launch. The company develops in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing (ISAM) technology — systems that can travel to satellites already in orbit, inspect them, dock with them, refuel them, and extend their operational lives.

https://x.com/TheRocketMediaX/status/2093994637488779731

Satellites are expensive assets that support everything from telecommunications and defence to weather tracking and GPS navigation. When one runs out of fuel or develops a fault, it is typically abandoned, even if most of its hardware still works. Many of these defunct satellites add to the growing problem of orbital debris. InspeCity's technology is designed to prevent that.

Its main platform, VEDA (Vehicle for Life Extension and Deorbiting Activities), integrates four proprietary subsystems: GITA for propulsion and mobility, CHAKSU for AI-enabled sensing and proximity operations, RAMA for robotic manipulation, and SPARSH for autonomous docking and in-orbit propellant transfer.

"Satellite life-extension is the first major problem we are solving, but the ability to inspect, approach, dock with, manipulate, refuel, and maintain spacecraft is foundational to a much larger in-space economy."

— Prof. Arindrajit Chowdhury, Founder and CEO, InspeCity

Four Missions in 18 Months

The fresh capital will fund InspeCity's transition from laboratory testing to orbital demonstration. The company plans to execute four in-orbit missions across its RIG-X, VEDA-X and SAMA-X roadmap over the next 12 to 18 months, progressively validating propulsion, sensing, autonomous operations, robotics, docking and refuelling capabilities in actual space conditions.

In parallel, InspeCity will scale commercial deployment of its GITA propulsion systems and expand its engineering, manufacturing and mission execution teams. The company's propulsion system has already cleared functional and environmental testing, including checks at ISRO laboratories.

Its technology stack has also received validation through India's defence innovation ecosystem, including the Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) programme.

India's Space Sector Heats Up

The fundraise lands at a moment of surging investor interest in Indian spacetech. In May 2026, Skyroot Aerospace became India's first spacetech unicorn after a $60 million round. GalaxEye raised Rs 44.2 crore in April, and Bellatrix Aerospace secured $20 million the same month. India's space economy is projected to reach $44 billion by 2033.

Globally, InspeCity competes in a niche occupied by firms like Japan's Astroscale, US-based Starfish Space and Orbit Fab, and Northrop Grumman's Mission Extension Vehicle programme. But its investors argue it holds an edge on cost.

"InspeCity has built the full stack — propulsion, robotics and RPOD — in-house, which is rare anywhere in the world and rarer still at this cost base. India has spent a decade proving it can put things into orbit affordably. The next decade is about what we can do once they're up there."

— Vishesh Rajaram, Managing Partner, Speciale Invest

The Bigger Vision

InspeCity's long-term thesis, which the founders call "Earth 2.0," looks far beyond satellite repair. The company envisions building infrastructure for sustained economic activity in space — eventually, orbital habitats capable of supporting large populations. For now, that vision is a North Star guiding near-term engineering choices.

Prof. Chowdhury, who continues to teach at IIT Bombay while leading the company, framed it plainly: "The ambition has not become smaller. The pathway has become much more specific." The next year and a half will determine whether InspeCity can turn laboratory prototypes into flight-qualified hardware — and whether India can stake its claim in the emerging business of keeping space clean and operational.

nri_angle: Founded by IIT Bombay alumni, InspeCity represents India's growing claim in the global space economy. Its success signals that deep-tech hardware startups incubated at Indian institutions can compete with international players like Astroscale and Northrop Grumman.
